name: The Iliad
author: Homer

claims.text: The Iliad covers roughly fifty days in the final year of the siege of Troy.
Its formulaic diction reflects oral compositional technique.
It reached approximately its present form in the 8th or 7th century BC.
Some described objects reflect genuine Bronze Age material culture.
A single poet composed the Iliad and the Odyssey.
Milman Parry established the theory of oral-formulaic composition in the 1930s partly by fieldwork recording living South Slavic epic singers in the Balkans.
Alexandrian scholars, especially Aristarchus of Samothrace, produced critical editions of the Iliad in the Hellenistic period that shaped the text later readers inherited.

summary: Fifty-one days in the tenth year of the Trojan War, framed entirely by the rage of Achilles and its consequences.
body:
The Iliad is not the story of the Trojan War. It opens in the tenth year with a quarrel over a captive woman, and ends before the city falls, with the burial of Hector. The wooden horse is not in it.

What it is about is stated in the first word: *mēnis*, wrath. Achilles withdraws, his friend Patroclus dies wearing his armour, and he returns to kill Hector in a rage that carries him past any recognisable limit — dragging the body behind his chariot for days.

The last book is the answer to the first. Priam comes alone at night to the tent of the man who killed his son, and kisses his hands. They weep together, and Achilles gives the body back. A poem about rage ends in shared grief between enemies, which is why it has never stopped being read.

The formulaic language — "swift-footed Achilles", "rosy-fingered dawn" — is the working technique of oral composition in performance rather than decorative style. Milman Parry demonstrated this in the 1930s not just through analysis of the Greek text but through direct fieldwork, travelling to the Balkans with Albert Lord to record living South Slavic epic singers who could improvise poems of comparable length in performance using exactly the same kind of reusable formulaic phrases scaled to fit the metre — evidence that this was a genuine technique for composing long poetry aloud without writing, not merely a stylistic quirk of a literate author imitating oral style.

How the poem then reached the fixed text later antiquity read is its own long story. Once writing made a stable version possible, the text still had centuries to drift before Hellenistic scholars at Alexandria, above all Aristarchus of Samothrace in the second century BC, produced critical editions comparing multiple manuscript traditions and marking lines they judged spurious rather than silently deleting them — an editorial caution that means variant readings from before Aristarchus' time still turn up in surviving papyri, giving modern scholars a rare window onto just how much the text could still vary before ancient scholarship settled it into something close to the version read today.

name: The Odyssey
author: Homer

claims.text: The Odyssey employs a non-linear narrative structure with embedded first-person narration.
It was composed somewhat later than the Iliad.
The two epics differ measurably in vocabulary and moral emphasis.
Odysseus' voyages can be mapped to real Mediterranean locations.

Emily Wilson's 2018 translation was the first published English rendering of the Odyssey by a woman, and rendered the poem's opening word polytropos as "complicated" rather than the traditional "man of many wiles" or "twists and turns".

The Victorian novelist Samuel Butler controversially argued the Odyssey was written by a young Sicilian woman, a theory almost no modern specialist accepts but which remains a well-known episode in the poem's reception history.

summary: Odysseus' ten-year journey home from Troy, and the reclaiming of a household that has almost given him up.
body:
The Odyssey is a different kind of poem from the Iliad: domestic rather than martial, structurally intricate, and interested in survival by cunning rather than glory by death.

Its hero lies constantly, and the poem admires him for it. He tells the Cyclops his name is Nobody; he tests his own household in disguise; he is introduced as *polytropos*, the man of many turns. The moral universe is less absolute than the Iliad's.

It is also the first European narrative to use non-linear structure. It begins near the end, spends four books on Telemachus before Odysseus appears, and has the hero narrate his own adventures at a feast — a flashback within a first-person account.

Penelope is the other half of the story. She holds off a hundred suitors for years by unweaving a shroud each night, and when Odysseus returns she tests him with a lie about their bed. She is as careful and as strategic as he is.

The poem's opening word, *polytropos*, describing Odysseus himself, has become a small battleground of its own in translation history precisely because it resists any single English equivalent: older translations rendered it as "the man of many wiles" or "of many turns," emphasising cunning, while Emily Wilson's widely read 2018 translation — the first published English version of the poem by a woman — chose the plainer and more ambiguous "complicated," a translation choice that shifts the poem's very first line toward psychological description rather than heroic epithet. The question of who actually composed the poem has its own long, mostly abandoned side-branch: the Victorian novelist Samuel Butler argued at length that internal evidence pointed to a young Sicilian noblewoman as the Odyssey's true author, a theory virtually no specialist today accepts but one still cited as a curiosity of the poem's reception, not least because the poem's sustained, sympathetic attention to Penelope's household and to the practicalities of weaving, textiles and domestic management struck Butler, and has struck some readers since, as more attentive to a woman's world than the Iliad's battlefield ever is.

name: Theogony
author: Hesiod

claims.text: The Theogony traces divine genealogy from Chaos to the rule of Zeus.
Its succession myth structurally parallels Hittite and Babylonian narratives.
It contains the earliest full accounts of Prometheus and Pandora.

summary: The genealogy of the gods from Chaos to the reign of Zeus — Greek religion's closest thing to a systematic cosmogony.
body:
The poem begins with Chaos, then Gaia (Earth), then Eros, and proceeds by generation. Ouranos imprisons his children; Gaia arms Kronos, who castrates him; Kronos swallows his own children; Zeus, hidden at birth, overthrows him. Power passes by violence three times before it stabilises.

The structure closely parallels the Hittite *Song of Kumarbi* and the Babylonian *Enuma Elish*, which makes it a key piece of evidence for Near Eastern influence on early Greek thought.

It is also where Prometheus steals fire and Pandora is created as the punishment — in Hesiod's telling, the origin of every trouble that afflicts men, in a poem noticeably hostile to women.

name: Works and Days
author: Hesiod

claims.text: Works and Days is addressed to Hesiod's brother in an inheritance dispute.
It contains detailed practical instruction on farming and craft.
It presents the myth of five successive declining ages.
It is the earliest surviving Greek poem with an identified personal narrator.

summary: A farming almanac addressed to the poet's dishonest brother — and the first personal voice in European literature.
body:
Hesiod addresses his brother Perses, who bribed the local "gift-devouring kings" to take more than his share of their inheritance. What follows is advice, complaint and moral argument in roughly equal measure.

The practical content is genuine: when to plough, when to harvest, how to build a plough and a wagon, which days are lucky. It is our best source for how an ordinary Greek farm actually worked.

Interleaved is the myth of the Five Ages — gold, silver, bronze, heroes, iron — declining to Hesiod's own miserable present. It is the earliest surviving European statement that the past was better, and it has never gone out of fashion.

What makes it new is the *I*. Homer never appears in his poems. Hesiod names himself, names his village, describes his father's failed emigration, and grumbles about the weather.

name: The Homeric Hymns
author: Various, anonymous

claims.text: The Homeric Hymns use Homeric metre and dialect but are not by Homer.
The Hymn to Demeter is the principal early source for the Persephone myth.
They were probably performed as preludes to longer epic recitation.

summary: Thirty-three hexameter hymns to individual gods — preludes to epic recitation, and the fullest early narratives of several myths.
body:
They are called Homeric because they use Homer's metre and dialect, not because he wrote them. Most were probably performed as preludes before longer epic recitations.

The long ones are substantial poems. The *Hymn to Demeter* is the primary source for the Eleusinian myth: Persephone taken by Hades, Demeter's search and grief, the failed harvest, and the pomegranate seeds that bind her to return each year. It is effectively the charter myth of the Mysteries.

The *Hymn to Hermes* is a comedy: the god steals Apollo's cattle hours after being born, drives them backwards to confuse the tracks, invents the lyre from a tortoise shell, and then talks his way out of trouble by giving Apollo the instrument.

name: The fragments of Sappho
author: Sappho
survival: One near-complete poem; c. 200 fragments, many from papyri

claims.text: Only one poem by Sappho survives essentially complete.
Much of the surviving corpus was recovered from Egyptian papyri.
Fragment 31 describes physical symptoms of desire and was widely imitated.
The loss of her work resulted mainly from changing transmission rather than deliberate destruction.
Recently published fragments are of secure provenance.

summary: The surviving remains of nine books of lyric poetry — the most celebrated love poetry of antiquity, in pieces.
body:
Of an estimated 10,000 lines, roughly 650 survive. Only the *Hymn to Aphrodite* is essentially complete: a prayer in which the goddess arrives smiling and asks, with visible amusement, who Sappho wants this time.

Fragment 31 describes the physical experience of watching a beloved talk to someone else — the tongue breaking, fire under the skin, a ringing in the ears, "greener than grass". It has been imitated for 2,600 years and is still the standard against which such poems are measured.

Most of what we have comes from two sources: quotations by later grammarians, and papyrus scraps excavated from Egyptian rubbish dumps at Oxyrhynchus, some recovered from mummy cartonnage. New fragments were published as recently as 2014, though one group's provenance has since been seriously questioned.

The loss is not primarily Christian censorship, as often claimed. Aeolic dialect fell out of the school curriculum, and works that stopped being copied simply stopped existing.

name: The Histories
author: Herodotus

claims.text: The Histories investigates the causes of the Greco-Persian Wars.
Herodotus distinguishes explicitly between reporting and believing his sources.
Several of his ethnographic descriptions have been confirmed archaeologically.
His army and casualty figures are systematically exaggerated.
He personally visited all the regions he describes.

summary: An enquiry into why Greeks and Persians went to war, which becomes an account of the whole known world.
body:
Herodotus sets out to preserve human achievements from oblivion and to explain the cause of the conflict. Getting there takes him through Egyptian mummification, Scythian cannabis vapour baths, Babylonian marriage auctions, Indian gold-digging ants and the circumnavigation of Africa by Phoenicians — who reported the sun on their right hand going west, which he disbelieves and which proves they did it.

His method is explicit and unusual: he reports what he was told, names his informants where he can, gives competing versions, and repeatedly states that he is obliged to record what is said but not to believe it.

He was called the father of lies in antiquity, and archaeology has vindicated him surprisingly often — on Scythian burial customs, on Egyptian practice, and on the Athos canal. His numbers, especially army sizes, are consistently far too large.

name: History of the Peloponnesian War
author: Thucydides
survival: Incomplete; breaks off mid-sentence in book eight

claims.text: Thucydides excluded divine causation from his historical explanation.
The work breaks off unfinished in 411 BC.
He states that the speeches represent what was appropriate rather than verbatim record.
He was an eyewitness to the plague and an Athenian commander.
His account is free of Athenian bias.

summary: The war between Athens and Sparta, analysed without gods, omens or consolation — the founding work of critical history.
body:
Thucydides announces his method against Herodotus: he has excluded the marvellous, cross-checked eyewitness accounts, and accepts that this makes the work less pleasant to hear. He intends it as "a possession for all time".

Its most quoted passages are structural analyses of political behaviour. The Melian Dialogue strips diplomacy to its mechanism — the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must — in an exchange that ends with Athens killing every man on Melos. The account of civil war at Corcyra describes how the meanings of words change under factional violence, so that recklessness becomes courage and moderation becomes cowardice.

The speeches are the central methodological problem. He admits he could not remember exact words and gives what the situation demanded, which makes them analysis in the mouths of participants.

It stops mid-sentence in 411 BC.

name: The Oresteia
author: Aeschylus
survival: Complete trilogy — the only one to survive

claims.text: The Oresteia is the only complete Greek tragic trilogy to survive.
It was produced in 458 BC and won first prize.
It stages the replacement of blood vengeance by a civic court.
It engages with contemporary reforms of the Areopagus.

summary: Three plays tracing a cycle of blood vengeance to its end in the first court of law.
body:
*Agamemnon*: the king returns from Troy and is murdered in his bath by his wife Clytemnestra, who has waited ten years and has her reasons — he sacrificed their daughter Iphigenia to get a favourable wind.

*The Libation Bearers*: their son Orestes returns and kills his mother, on Apollo's instruction, and is immediately pursued by the Furies.

*The Eumenides*: Orestes is tried at Athens before a jury of citizens with Athena presiding. The vote is tied; Athena casts for acquittal. The Furies, enraged, are persuaded to accept a new role as honoured guardians of justice within the city.

The trilogy dramatises a transition: from private vengeance, where every killing demands another, to public law, where a verdict ends the matter. It was staged shortly after the Areopagus court had been controversially reformed, so the argument was live.

name: Oedipus Rex
author: Sophocles

claims.text: Aristotle treated Oedipus Rex as the model of tragic plot construction.
The play uses sustained dramatic irony based on audience foreknowledge.
It did not win first prize on its original production.
It was written in response to the plague of Athens.

summary: A king investigating a plague discovers that he is himself the cause — the most tightly constructed plot in Greek drama.
body:
Thebes is dying of plague. The oracle says the killer of the previous king must be found. Oedipus takes charge of the investigation with total confidence, and every step towards the truth is a step towards his destruction.

The irony is structural rather than decorative: the audience knows from the start, so every confident statement Oedipus makes lands differently for them than for him. He curses the killer without qualification. He mocks the blind prophet Teiresias for not seeing.

Aristotle used it in the *Poetics* as his model of plot construction, singling out the messenger scene where the news intended to reassure Oedipus is precisely what destroys him — *peripeteia* and *anagnorisis* arriving in the same moment.

Freud took the name for his complex, which has coloured every subsequent reading. The play itself is about knowledge, not desire: Oedipus is destroyed by finding out.

name: Antigone
author: Sophocles

claims.text: Antigone stages a conflict between religious obligation and civic decree.
It was produced around 441 BC.
The play has been repeatedly adapted as political resistance literature.
Sophocles presents both Antigone and Creon as partly justified.

summary: A woman buries her brother against the king's edict — the founding text of the conflict between conscience and law.
body:
Creon forbids burial of Polynices, who attacked the city. Antigone, his sister, buries him anyway, invoking the unwritten and unfailing laws of the gods. Creon condemns her to be walled up alive.

Hegel's reading is the influential one and remains persuasive: this is not right against wrong but right against right. Creon has a genuine case — the city must survive, and traitors cannot be honoured — and it is destroyed by his refusal to bend. Antigone is equally absolute and equally destructive, dismissing her sister's offer of help with contempt.

Creon relents too late. Antigone has hanged herself; his son, betrothed to her, kills himself; his wife follows. He is left alive, which is the harsher outcome.

The play has been used as a resistance text under occupations and dictatorships repeatedly — Anouilh staged it in occupied Paris in 1944, and both the Resistance and the censors approved.

name: Medea
author: Euripides

claims.text: Medea was produced in 431 BC and placed third in the competition.
It contains an extended speech on the condition of married women.
Medea escapes without punishment at the end of the play.
Euripides invented the version in which Medea kills her own children.

summary: A foreign woman, abandoned by the husband she made a king, takes a revenge that destroys her own children.
body:
Medea helped Jason steal the Golden Fleece, betrayed her father, killed her brother, and killed his enemy for him. He now sets her aside to marry a Corinthian princess, and expects gratitude for the connection.

Her speech to the women of Corinth on the position of wives — bought with a dowry into a stranger's house, judged for a choice they cannot inspect beforehand, and told they live safe at home while men fight — is the most direct statement on the subject in Greek literature. She would rather stand three times in battle, she says, than bear one child.

Then she poisons the princess and her father, and kills her own two sons, and escapes in a chariot sent by her grandfather the Sun. Euripides gives her no punishment and no repentance. The play ends with Jason destroyed and Medea in the air above him.

It placed third of three.

name: The Republic
author: Plato

claims.text: The Republic constructs an ideal city to investigate the nature of justice in the soul.
It advocates rule by philosopher-kings and censorship of poetry.
It argues that women should be eligible for guardianship and education.
Plato intended it as a practical political programme.

summary: A dialogue that builds an ideal city in order to answer a question about the individual soul: is it better to be just?
body:
The question is posed sharply by Glaucon: given a ring of invisibility, would anyone remain just? To answer, Socrates proposes examining justice writ large, in a city, and then reading the result back onto the soul.

The city that emerges is not attractive. Poetry is censored, including Homer. Rulers lie for the public good. Guardians hold property and reproduction in common, with children taken at birth. Citizens are assigned to classes and told a "noble lie" about the metal in their souls to keep them there. Reading it as a blueprint for a good society, as Karl Popper did, produces an authoritarian text — and the text supplies the material.

It also contains the Allegory of the Cave, the Divided Line, the theory of Forms, and the first sustained argument in Western philosophy that women should receive the same education and hold the same offices as men.

name: Poetics
author: Aristotle

claims.text: The Poetics analyses tragedy in terms of six constituent parts, with plot primary.
It introduces the concepts of hamartia, peripeteia, anagnorisis and catharsis.
The book dealing with comedy is lost.
Catharsis means the purgation of emotion rather than intellectual clarification.

summary: The founding work of literary criticism, which analyses tragedy as a mechanism and asks what it does to an audience.
body:
Aristotle treats poetry as a craft with parts that can be examined. Tragedy imitates a serious action, through plot, character, thought, diction, song and spectacle, and its plot is the most important part — character exists for the sake of the action, not the reverse.

He introduces *hamartia* (the error that brings a good man down, not a moral flaw), *peripeteia* (reversal), *anagnorisis* (recognition) and *catharsis* — the purging or clarification of pity and fear, which he never fully explains and which has been argued over for 2,300 years.

He also says poetry is more philosophical than history, because history records what happened while poetry shows what would happen — the universal rather than the particular.

The second book, on comedy, is lost. Its absence is the premise of Umberto Eco's *The Name of the Rose*.

name: Nicomachean Ethics
author: Aristotle

claims.text: The Ethics identifies eudaimonia as the human good and defines virtue as a mean between extremes.
It holds that virtue is acquired through habituation rather than instruction alone.
Two of its ten books are devoted to friendship.
It is the founding text of the virtue-ethics tradition.

summary: An investigation of how to live well, arguing that virtue is a skill acquired by practice rather than a rule to be learned.
body:
Aristotle starts from the fact that everyone agrees the goal is *eudaimonia* — flourishing, faring well — and disagrees entirely about what it consists of. His answer is activity of the soul in accordance with virtue, over a complete life.

Virtue is a disposition lying between excess and deficiency, relative to the person and the situation: courage between recklessness and cowardice, generosity between waste and meanness. It cannot be reduced to rules, because the right response depends on circumstances, and it is acquired by habituation — we become just by doing just acts, as we become builders by building.

He devotes two full books to friendship, more than to any other single topic, distinguishing friendships of utility, pleasure and character, and arguing that only the last is complete.

The work founded virtue ethics, which after two centuries of rule-based moral philosophy has become a major live position again.

name: The Philippics
author: Demosthenes

claims.text: Demosthenes delivered a series of speeches against Philip II between 351 and 341 BC.
He argued that Athens must fund and serve in campaigns directly rather than rely on mercenaries.
The term "philippic" became a generic name for a denunciatory speech.
The published speeches match what was actually delivered.

summary: Speeches warning Athens that Philip of Macedon was an existential threat — the finest Greek oratory, and unheeded.
body:
Demosthenes' argument is consistent across a decade: Philip is not a conventional rival who can be managed, but an opponent who campaigns in winter, does not stop for festivals, uses mercenaries and bribery, and will take everything unless resisted now.

He is at his sharpest attacking his own citizens' behaviour. Athenians, he says, wander around the marketplace asking each other for news — is Philip dead? is he ill? — as though the outcome depended on rumour rather than on what they do. They vote for expeditions and do not serve in them.

The speeches failed. Athens acted too late and lost at Chaeronea in 338 BC.

The name became generic: Cicero called his attacks on Mark Antony *Philippics*, and was killed for them. As rhetoric they were studied as models for two thousand years.

name: Anabasis of Alexander
author: Arrian of Nicomedia

claims.text: Arrian based his account principally on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, both eyewitnesses.
Both of his principal sources are otherwise lost.
His military description is generally regarded as the most reliable of the Alexander historians.
His account is favourable to Alexander.

summary: The most reliable surviving account of Alexander's campaigns, written four centuries later from participants' memoirs.
body:
Arrian was a Roman-era Greek administrator and soldier who chose his sources deliberately: Ptolemy, who was there and became a king and therefore, Arrian reasons, had less reason to lie; and Aristobulus, an engineer on the campaign. Both works are lost, so Arrian is our access to them.

His military detail is credible in a way the other accounts are not — he had commanded troops and understood formations, supply and terrain. Where his sources disagree he says so.

He is not neutral. He admires Alexander and treats the murder of Cleitus and the execution of Parmenion as lapses in an otherwise great man rather than as evidence about his character. But he flags what he cannot verify, and marks the difference between what is reported and what he believes — which is more than Curtius or Diodorus do.

name: Life of Alexander
author: Plutarch

claims.text: Plutarch explicitly distinguishes biography from history in his stated method.
The Life of Alexander is paired with the Life of Julius Caesar.
Plutarch preserves anecdotes from sources now lost.
Shakespeare drew directly on translations of Plutarch for several plays.

summary: A biography paired with Julius Caesar, explicitly interested in character rather than military narrative.
body:
Plutarch states his method at the outset: he is writing lives, not histories, and a small thing — a phrase, a joke — often reveals character better than a battle with thousands dead.

So he gives us the young Alexander taming Bucephalus by noticing the horse is frightened of its own shadow; the Gordian knot; the letter to Aristotle complaining that publishing his teachings has robbed Alexander of his advantage; the drunken killing of Cleitus and the days of remorse afterwards.

The method has real costs. Plutarch is writing 400 years later, moralising, and does not always distinguish anecdote from evidence. But he preserves material from lost sources, and his psychological interest in his subjects gives a portrait Arrian does not attempt.

He wrote fifty *Parallel Lives*, pairing a Greek and a Roman, and the collection shaped how Europe imagined antiquity — Shakespeare took the plots of three plays almost directly from North's translation.

name: Parallel Lives
author: Plutarch

claims.text: Parallel Lives pairs Greek and Roman figures with explicit comparisons.
Plutarch states a moral rather than historical purpose.
The work preserves material from sources now lost.
It was a major influence on Renaissance and Enlightenment political thought.

summary: Fifty biographies pairing a Greek with a Roman, comparing their characters — the main channel through which antiquity reached Renaissance Europe.
body:
Each pair is followed by a short comparison: Alexander with Caesar, Demosthenes with Cicero, Theseus with Romulus. The point is moral rather than historical — Plutarch wants readers to examine their own conduct against these examples, and says so.

Because he wrote in the Roman imperial period with access to libraries now lost, he is often our only source for particular events and for whole lost works.

His influence on later Europe is hard to overstate. Shakespeare's *Julius Caesar*, *Antony and Cleopatra* and *Coriolanus* follow North's Plutarch closely, sometimes verbatim. Montaigne, Rousseau and the leaders of the French and American revolutions all read him as a manual of public virtue.

name: Bibliotheca historica
author: Diodorus Siculus

claims.text: The Bibliotheca is a universal history compiled in the 1st century BC.
Books 11–20 survive complete and cover 480–302 BC.
It preserves material from historians whose works are otherwise lost.
Its chronology and internal consistency are unreliable.

summary: A universal history from mythical times to Caesar, valuable chiefly because it copies sources that no longer exist.
body:
Diodorus is not a distinguished historian. He compiles rather than analyses, contradicts himself between books because he is following different sources, and his chronology is unreliable.

He is nonetheless indispensable. Books 11–20 cover 480–302 BC continuously, and for the wars of the Diadochi he is the main narrative we have, drawing on Hieronymus of Cardia — a participant whose own work is lost. His account of Philip II depends on Ephorus and Theopompus, also lost.

This is the normal condition of ancient history: the good writers vanish and the compilers survive, so the evidence often reaches us through someone who did not fully understand it. Reading Diodorus means reading through him to the better source underneath.

name: The Histories
author: Polybius
survival: Books 1–5 complete; the rest in excerpts

claims.text: Polybius set out to explain Roman expansion between 220 and 167 BC.
Book 6 analyses the Roman constitution as a mixed form with mutual checks.
He argued that historians require practical political and military experience.
His constitutional analysis influenced later republican political theory.

summary: An analysis of how Rome conquered the Mediterranean in fifty-three years, by a Greek who watched it from inside.
body:
Polybius asks a single question: how, and by what kind of constitution, did Rome bring almost the whole inhabited world under its rule in less than fifty-three years?

His answer is institutional. Book 6 analyses the Roman constitution as a mixture of monarchy (consuls), aristocracy (senate) and democracy (assemblies), each checking the others so that the cycle of constitutional decay is slowed. This analysis reached Montesquieu and, through him, the framers of the American constitution.

He also gives the classic technical comparison of legion and phalanx, and insists that history must be written by people with practical political and military experience — he had both, and had been deported to Rome as a hostage after his side lost.

He demands that historians travel to the places they describe and interrogate participants, and attacks those who write from libraries.

name: The Elements
author: Euclid

claims.text: The Elements derives geometrical results from a small set of stated postulates.
It includes a proof that the primes are infinite in number.
It remained a standard mathematics textbook into the 20th century.
The parallel postulate is logically independent of the other four.

summary: Thirteen books deriving all of Greek geometry from five postulates — the most successful textbook ever written.
body:
The *Elements* is not primarily a collection of results; it is a demonstration of method. Twenty-three definitions, five postulates and five common notions are laid out, and everything that follows is proved from them, with each proposition depending only on what has already been established.

Book I ends with the Pythagorean theorem. Book IX proves that there are infinitely many primes — assume a finite list, multiply them all together and add one, and the result is either prime or has a prime factor not on the list. Book X treats irrational magnitudes; Book XIII constructs the five Platonic solids and proves there are no others.

It was a standard school text into the twentieth century, and Lincoln reportedly read it to learn what it meant to demonstrate something.

The fifth postulate, about parallels, is conspicuously less obvious than the others. Two thousand years of attempts to derive it from the rest failed, and in the nineteenth century Lobachevsky, Bolyai and Riemann showed why: deny it and you get consistent alternative geometries — the ones general relativity turned out to need.

name: Argonautica
author: Apollonius of Rhodes

claims.text: The Argonautica retells the voyage for the Golden Fleece in four books.
Book 3 gives an extended psychological portrait of Medea in love.
It directly influenced Virgil's treatment of Dido in the Aeneid.
Apollonius quarrelled with Callimachus over epic poetry.

summary: Jason's voyage for the Golden Fleece, retold as a Hellenistic epic with a psychologically realistic heroine.
body:
Apollonius wrote epic in an age that thought epic was finished. His answer to the problem is to make the hero inadequate: Jason is repeatedly at a loss, frequently rescued by others, and succeeds mainly through Medea.

Book 3 is the innovation. It follows Medea falling in love — sleepless, arguing with herself, going to her sister and losing her nerve, deciding to help this stranger betray her own father. It is the first extended interior portrait of a person in love in European literature, and Virgil takes it directly for Dido in the *Aeneid*.

The poem also displays Alexandrian scholarship: obscure geography, aetiologies for local customs, learned digressions. Callimachus is said to have disapproved of long poems, and the two are supposed to have quarrelled over it, though that story may be a later invention.

name: The Idylls
author: Theocritus

claims.text: Theocritus originated the pastoral genre in Greek poetry.
His pastoral world was written for an urban Alexandrian audience.
The Idylls directly influenced Virgil's Eclogues.
Some poems in the collection are not by Theocritus.

summary: Short poems of herdsmen singing in the Sicilian countryside — the invention of pastoral poetry.
body:
Theocritus wrote for an urban, educated audience at Alexandria, imagining a rural world of goatherds competing in song under trees. The countryside in his poems is a literary construction, and everyone involved knew it — which is exactly what pastoral has always been.

The form runs directly to Virgil's *Eclogues*, then to Renaissance pastoral, Milton's *Lycidas*, Shelley's *Adonais* and the whole tradition of the elegy set among shepherds.

Not all the Idylls are rural. Idyll 15 follows two Syracusan housewives through the crowds of Alexandria to a festival, complaining about their husbands, the traffic and a man who tells them to stop talking. It is one of the liveliest depictions of ordinary urban life anywhere in Greek literature.

name: The Septuagint
author: Jewish scholars at Alexandria

claims.text: The Hebrew scriptures were translated into Greek at Alexandria beginning in the 3rd century BC.
The translation was produced gradually over roughly 150 years by multiple translators.
New Testament authors generally quote the Greek rather than the Hebrew text.
The account of seventy-two independent identical translations is legendary.

summary: The Hebrew scriptures translated into Greek at Alexandria — the first major translation of a sacred text in history.
body:
Alexandria's Jewish community was large and increasingly Greek-speaking, and needed the scriptures in a language it could read. The Torah was translated first, in the third century BC, and the rest followed over roughly 150 years.

The name comes from a legend recorded in the Letter of Aristeas: seventy-two scholars worked separately and produced identical texts. The legend is doing theological work — it certifies the translation as divinely guided — and the actual process was clearly gradual and uneven, with different books showing markedly different translation styles.

Its consequences were enormous. It made Jewish scripture readable across the Hellenistic world, and it is the version quoted by the New Testament writers, so its Greek vocabulary shaped Christian theology. Where the Hebrew *almah* (young woman) was rendered as *parthenos* (virgin) in Isaiah, the translation choice acquired doctrinal weight it could not have carried in the original.
